title: What are Sequenced Collections (Java 21 — `SequencedCollection`/`SequencedSet`/`SequencedMap`, getFirst/getLast/reversed), and what gap did they fill?
shortTitle: What are Sequenced Collections (Java 21), and what gap did they fill?

s1_definition.profdef: Sequenced Collections, added in Java 21, are three new interfaces, `SequencedCollection`, `SequencedSet`, and `SequencedMap`, that give a uniform API to any collection with a defined encounter order. They add first and last access and mutation methods such as `getFirst`, `getLast`, `addFirst`, `addLast`, `removeFirst`, `removeLast`, and a `reversed` view, and `SequencedMap` adds `firstEntry`, `lastEntry`, `pollFirstEntry`, `pollLastEntry`, `putFirst`, `putLast`, and `reversed`. They were retrofitted into existing types like `List`, `Deque`, `LinkedHashSet`, `LinkedHashMap`, and the `NavigableSet` and `NavigableMap` families, filling the long-standing gap that there was no common, consistent way to ask an ordered collection for its first or last element or to iterate it in reverse.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps several ordered queues: a line of customers at the counter, a ledger of transactions in date order, and a list of recent logins. Before Java 21, asking "who is first" and "who is last" worked differently for each: for one you called a method, for another you did size minus one, and for a set you had to iterate the whole thing just to reach the end. Sequenced Collections are like a single standard rule posted on every ordered queue: "to see the front, say getFirst; to see the back, say getLast; to read it backwards, say reversed." One consistent vocabulary for every ordered line in the bank.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sequenced Collections give every ordered collection one uniform API for first, last, and reversed access, filling the gap where getting the first or last element and reversing differed inconsistently across List, Deque, and ordered sets and maps.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sequenced Collections, added in Java 21, are three new interfaces, `SequencedCollection`, `SequencedSet`, and `SequencedMap`, that give a uniform API to any collection with a defined encounter order. They add first and last access and mutation methods such as `getFirst`, `getLast`, `addFirst`, `addLast`, `removeFirst`, `removeLast`, and a `reversed` view, and `SequencedMap` adds `firstEntry`, `lastEntry`, `pollFirstEntry`, `pollLastEntry`, `putFirst`, `putLast`, and `reversed`. They were retrofitted into existing types like `List`, `Deque`, `LinkedHashSet`, `LinkedHashMap`, and the `NavigableSet` and `NavigableMap` families, filling the long-standing gap that there was no common, consistent way to ask an ordered collection for its first or last element or to iterate it in reverse.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps several ordered queues: a line of customers at the counter, a ledger of transactions in date order, and a list of recent logins. Before Java 21, asking "who is first" and "who is last" worked differently for each: for one you called a method, for another you did size minus one, and for a set you had to iterate the whole thing just to reach the end. Sequenced Collections are like a single standard rule posted on every ordered queue: "to see the front, say getFirst; to see the back, say getLast; to read it backwards, say reversed." One consistent vocabulary for every ordered line in the bank.

**One line to remember:** Sequenced Collections give every ordered collection one uniform API for first, last, and reversed access, filling the gap where getting the first or last element and reversing differed inconsistently across List, Deque, and ordered sets and maps.

sections.s2_technical:
Before Java 21, order was a concept scattered across types with no shared interface. A List could give its first element with get of zero and its last with get of size minus one. A Deque had getFirst and getLast. A LinkedHashSet had a defined iteration order but no direct way to get the last element except iterating to the end, and getting the first meant starting an iterator. A LinkedHashMap and a sorted map had order too, but accessing the ends was inconsistent. Reversing an ordered collection usually meant copying or writing manual loops. There was simply no single type that said "I have a well-defined first and last."

Sequenced Collections fix this with a small hierarchy. SequencedCollection is the base, adding getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast, and reversed. SequencedSet extends it for sets with unique elements and refines reversed to return a SequencedSet. SequencedMap is the map counterpart with firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, pollLastEntry, putFirst, putLast, and reversed that returns a SequencedMap. These were retrofitted so that List and Deque now implement SequencedCollection, LinkedHashSet and the NavigableSet family implement SequencedSet, and LinkedHashMap and the NavigableMap family implement SequencedMap, so existing collections gained the new methods without you changing their types.

The reversed view is the elegant part: it returns a view, not a copy, so iterating it walks the original in reverse and, for mutable collections, changes through the view write back to the original. For example a List of transactions lets me call `txns.getLast()` for the most recent and `txns.reversed()` to iterate newest first, and a LinkedHashSet of recent account ids lets me call `recent.getLast()` directly instead of iterating. A senior nuance: the methods carry the obvious contracts, so getFirst and getLast throw NoSuchElementException on an empty collection, and addFirst or addLast on a sorted set or map that orders by comparator will throw UnsupportedOperationException because you cannot force a position against the sort order. The feature adds no new data structures; it is purely a unifying API layered over existing ordered types, which is exactly why it is valuable: it removes a pile of index arithmetic and iterator boilerplate and makes ordered-collection code read the same everywhere.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India keeps an ordered list of a customer's transactions and frequently needs the most recent one and a newest-first view for the statement. The old code used size minus one and manual reverse loops, which was noisy and easy to get wrong on empty lists. This is exactly what SequencedCollection solves — getLast and reversed in a uniform, safe API.

Problem 2 — The bank keeps a LinkedHashSet of recently used account ids in insertion order and a LinkedHashMap of recent logins, and getting the first or last of these meant awkward iteration. This is exactly what SequencedSet and SequencedMap solve — firstEntry, lastEntry, getFirst, and getLast directly on the ordered set and map.

The demo uses a transaction list, a recent-accounts set, and a recent-logins map to show getFirst, getLast, addFirst, reversed, and the map entry accessors, including the empty-collection behavior. Classes and steps: `TransactionHistory` (wraps a List), `RecentActivity` (set and map), and `SequencedDemo`.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo

# Note: addFirst/addLast on a TreeSet/TreeMap (sorted by comparator) throw
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transactions of Rs.50,000, Rs.25,000, and Rs.10,000, plus two touched accounts and two logins for Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1 — Each transaction is appended with addLast, so the list holds them in order from oldest to newest. Asking for oldest returns the Rs.50,000 with getFirst and mostRecent returns the Rs.10,000 with getLast, with no index arithmetic and no risk of an off-by-one error.

Step 2 — printNewestFirst calls reversed, which returns a view over the same list walked backwards, so the statement shows Rs.10,000, Rs.25,000, Rs.50,000 without copying the data.

Step 3 — The recent-accounts LinkedHashSet is touched with SAV2001 then CUR3001, so firstTouched returns SAV2001 and lastTouched returns CUR3001 directly, which previously required iterating the set to reach the end.

Step 4 — The recent-logins LinkedHashMap reports its first and last entries with firstEntry and lastEntry and a reversed key view, and finally calling getLast on an empty history correctly throws NoSuchElementException, demonstrating the fail-fast contract on empty collections.

```
2026-10-26 16:15:01 [INFO] oldest=Rs.50000 mostRecent=Rs.10000
2026-10-26 16:15:01 [INFO] Newest-first: [10000, 25000, 50000]
2026-10-26 16:15:01 [INFO] firstTouched=SAV2001 lastTouched=CUR3001
2026-10-26 16:15:01 [INFO] first login entry = SAV2001=2026-10-26T16:15:01
2026-10-26 16:15:01 [INFO] last login entry  = CUR3001=2026-10-26T16:15:01
2026-10-26 16:15:01 [INFO] logins reversed    = [CUR3001, SAV2001]
2026-10-26 16:15:01 [WARNING] empty history: getLast() correctly threw NoSuchElementException
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  THE GAP (before Java 21)
    List:          first = get(0)           last = get(size()-1)
    Deque:         first = getFirst()       last = getLast()
    LinkedHashSet: first = iterator().next() last = iterate to end (!!)
    reverse:       copy or manual loop
    → no common interface for "ordered, has a first and last"

  SEQUENCED COLLECTIONS (Java 21) — one uniform API
    SequencedCollection: getFirst/getLast/addFirst/addLast/removeFirst/removeLast/reversed
       └─ SequencedSet  (LinkedHashSet, NavigableSet)
    SequencedMap:        firstEntry/lastEntry/pollFirst/pollLast/putFirst/putLast/reversed
       (LinkedHashMap, NavigableMap)

  record 50000,25000,10000 (addLast)
    getFirst → 50000   getLast → 10000   reversed (VIEW) → [10000,25000,50000]
  empty.getLast() → NoSuchElementException   TreeSet.addFirst() → UnsupportedOperationException
```

```
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Interface Segregation (retrofit): small first/last/reversed API│
  │    WHY: unify ordered types without new data structures        │
  │ View (reversed): lazy reverse view, no copy                    │

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ I: SequencedCollection/Set/Map are small, focused interfaces   │
  │ L: any ordered collection substitutes where first/last needed  │
  │ O: existing types gained methods without changing call types   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ SequencedCollection<E>        │ getFirst/getLast/addFirst/addLast/reversed
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
      implements  │  (retrofitted)
      ┌───────────┼───────────────┐
      ▼           ▼               ▼
    List        Deque        SequencedSet (LinkedHashSet, NavigableSet)

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ SequencedMap<K,V>             │ firstEntry/lastEntry/putFirst/putLast/reversed
  └──────────────────────────────┘  (LinkedHashMap, NavigableMap)

  ── Contracts (as prose) ──────────────────────────────────────
  getFirst/getLast on empty      : NoSuchElementException
  addFirst/addLast on sorted set : UnsupportedOperationException
  reversed()                     : a VIEW; mutations write back

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. record(amt) → txns.addLast(amt)
  2. mostRecent() → txns.getLast()
  3. printNewestFirst() → txns.reversed() (view)
  4. recentLogins.firstEntry()/lastEntry()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sequenced Collections, added in Java 21, are three new interfaces, SequencedCollection, SequencedSet, and SequencedMap, that give any collection with a defined encounter order one uniform API for first and last access and for reversal. The collection interface adds getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast, and a reversed view, and the map interface adds firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, pollLastEntry, putFirst, putLast, and reversed.

The gap they fill is that before Java 21, order was a concept scattered across types with no shared interface. A List gave its first element with get of zero and its last with get of size minus one. A Deque had getFirst and getLast. A LinkedHashSet had a defined iteration order but no direct way to reach the last element except iterating all the way to the end, and reversing an ordered collection usually meant copying it or writing a manual loop. There was simply no common type that said "I am ordered and I have a first and a last," so the same conceptual operation looked different everywhere.

These interfaces were retrofitted into the existing types, so List and Deque implement SequencedCollection, LinkedHashSet and the sorted-set family implement SequencedSet, and LinkedHashMap and the sorted-map family implement SequencedMap, all without my changing their types. The reversed method is especially elegant because it returns a view rather than a copy, so iterating it walks the original backwards and, on mutable collections, changes through the view write back to the original.

In my banking work at National Bank of India this cleaned up a lot of ordered-collection code. A customer's transaction list exposed the most recent transaction with getLast and a newest-first statement view with reversed, instead of size minus one and manual reverse loops that were easy to get wrong on empty lists. A LinkedHashSet of recently used accounts and a LinkedHashMap of recent logins gained direct first and last access instead of awkward iteration. The senior details I always add are that the methods carry the obvious contracts, so getFirst and getLast throw NoSuchElementException on an empty collection, and addFirst or addLast on a sorted set or map throws UnsupportedOperationException because you cannot force a position against the comparator's order, and that the feature adds no new data structures at all; it is purely a unifying API over existing ordered types, which is exactly why it is so useful for removing index arithmetic and iterator boilerplate.
